title: 216.402-470 Award fee reduction or denial for jeopardizing the health or
content:
L0:216.402-470 Award fee reduction or denial for jeopardizing the health or
L0:safety of Government personnel.
L1:(a) Definitions. As used in this section—
L0:“Covered incident” and “serious bodily injury,” are defined in the clause at 252.216-
L0:7004, Award Fee Reduction or Denial for Jeopardizing the Health or Safety of
L0:Government Personnel.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(b) The contracting officer must include in the evaluation criteria of any award-fee
L0:plan, a review of contractor and subcontractor actions that jeopardized the health or
L0:safety of Government personnel, through gross negligence or reckless disregard for the
L0:safety of such personnel, as determined through—
L1:(1) Conviction in a criminal proceeding, or finding of fault and liability in a civil
L0:or administrative proceeding (in accordance with section 823 of the National Defense
L0:Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year (FY) 2010 (Pub. L. 111-84)); or
L1:(2) If a contractor or a subcontractor at any tier is not subject to the jurisdiction
L0:of the U.S. courts, a final determination of contractor or subcontractor fault resulting
L0:from a DoD investigation (in accordance with section 834 of the NDAA for FY 2011
L0:(Pub. L. 111-383)).
L1:(c) In evaluating the contractor’s performance under a contract that includes the
L0:clause at 252.216-7004, Award Fee Reduction or Denial for Jeopardizing the Health or
L0:Safety of Government Personnel, the contracting officer must consider reducing or
L0:denying award fees for a period, if contractor or subcontractor actions cause serious
L0:bodily injury or death of civilian or military Government personnel during such period.
L0:The contracting officer’s evaluation must consider recovering all or part of award fees
L0:previously paid for such period.

L0:ECONOMIC PRICE ADJUSTMENT—BASIC STEEL, ALUMINUM, BRASS,

L1:(a) Definitions. As used in this clause—

L0:“Unit price” excludes any part of the price which reflects requirements for

L1:(b) As represented by the Contractor in its offer, the unit price stated for

L0:applying any applicable standard trade discounts offered by the Contractor from its

L1:(c) The Contractor shall promptly notify the Contracting Officer of the amount and

title: 252.216-7001 Economic Price Adjustment-Nonstandard Steel Items
content:
L0:252.216-7001 Economic Price Adjustment-Nonstandard Steel Items.
L0:As prescribed in 216.203-470(b), use the following clause:
L0:ECONOMIC PRICE ADJUSTMENT—NONSTANDARD STEEL ITEMS (JAN 2023)
L1:(a) Definitions. As used in this clause—
L0:“Base labor index” means the average of the labor indices for the three months
L0:which consist of the month of bid opening (or offer submission) and the months
L0:immediately preceding and following that month.
L0:“Base steel index” means the Contractor's established price (see Note 6) including all
L0:applicable extras of $________ per ____________ (see Note 1) for _______________ (see
L0:Note 2) on the date set for bid opening (or the date of submission of the offer).
L0:“Current labor index” means the average of the labor indices for the month in which
L0:delivery of supplies is required to be made and the month preceding.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:“Current steel index” means the Contractor's established price (see Note 6) for that
L0:item, including all applicable extras in effect ___ days (see Note 3) prior to the first day
L0:of the month in which delivery is required.
L0:“Established price” is—
L1:(1) A price which is an established catalog or market price of a commercial
L0:product sold in substantial quantities to the general public; and
L1:(2) The net price after applying any applicable standard trade discounts offered
L0:by the Contractor from its catalog, list, or schedule price. (But see Note 6.)
L0:“Labor index” means the average straight time hourly earnings of the Contractor's
L0:employees in the ____________ shop of the Contractor's ________________ plant (see
L0:Note 4) for any particular month.
L0:“Month” means calendar month. However, if the Contractor's accounting period does
L0:not coincide with the calendar month, then that accounting period shall be used in lieu
L0:of “month.”
L1:(b) Each contract unit price shall be subject to revision, under the terms of this
L0:clause, to reflect changes in the cost of labor and steel. For purpose of this price revision,
L0:the proportion of the contract unit price attributable to costs of labor not otherwise
L0:included in the price of the steel item identified under the “base steel index” definition
L0:in paragraph (a) shall be _____ percent, and the proportion of the contract unit price
L0:attributable to the cost of steel shall be _____ percent. (See Note 5.)
L2:(c)(1) Unless otherwise specified in this contract, the labor index shall be computed
L0:by dividing the total straight time earnings of the Contractor's employees in the shop
L0:identified in paragraph (a) for any given month by the total number of straight time
L0:hours worked by those employees in that month.
L1:(2) Any revision in a contract unit price to reflect changes in the cost of labor
L0:shall be computed solely by reference to the “base labor index” and the “current labor
L0:index.”
L1:(d) Any revision in a contract unit price to reflect changes in the cost of steel shall be
L0:computed solely by reference to the “base steel index” and the “current steel index.”
L2:(e)(1) Each contract unit price shall be revised for each month in which delivery of
L0:supplies is required to be made.
L1:(2) The revised contract unit price shall apply to the deliveries of those
L0:quantities required to be made in that month regardless of when actual delivery is
L0:made.
L1:(3) Each revised contract unit price shall be computed by adding—
L1:(i) The adjusted cost of labor (obtained by multiplying ____ percent of the
L0:contract unit price by a fraction, of which the numerator shall be the current labor index
L0:and the denominator shall be the base labor index);
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(ii) The adjusted cost of steel (obtained by multiplying ____ percent of the
L0:contract unit price by a fraction, of which the numerator shall be the current steel index
L0:and the denominator shall be the base steel index); and
L1:(iii) The amount equal to ____ percent of the original contract unit price
L0:(representing that portion of the unit price which relates neither to the cost of labor nor
L0:the cost of steel, and which is therefore not subject to revision (see Note 5)).
L1:(4) The aggregate of the increases in any contract unit price under this contract
L0:shall not exceed ten percent of the original contract unit price.
L1:(5) Computations shall be made to the nearest one-hundredth of one cent.
L2:(f)(1) Pending any revisions of the contract unit prices, the Contractor shall be paid
L0:the contract unit price for deliveries made.
L1:(2) Within 30 days after final delivery (or such other period as may be
L0:authorized by the Contracting Officer), the Contractor shall furnish a statement
L0:identifying the correctness of—
L1:(i) The average straight time hourly earnings of the Contractor's employees
L0:in the shop identified in paragraph (a) that are relevant to the computations of the
L0:“base labor index” and the “current labor index;” and
L1:(ii) The Contractor's established prices (see Note 6), including all applicable
L0:extras for like quantities of the item that are relevant to the computation of the “base
L0:steel index” and the “current steel index.”
L1:(3) Upon request of the Contracting Officer, the Contractor shall make available
L0:all records used in the computation of the labor indices.
L1:(4) Upon receipt of the statement, the Contracting Officer will compute the
L0:revised contract unit prices and modify the contract accordingly. No modification to this
L0:contract will be made pursuant to this clause until the Contracting Officer has verified
L0:the revised established price (see Note 6).
L2:(g)(1) In the event any item of this contract is subject to a total or partial termination
L0:for convenience, the month in which the Contractor receives notice of the termination, if
L0:prior to the month in which delivery is required, shall be considered the month in which
L0:delivery of the terminated item is required for the purposes of determining the current
L0:labor and steel indices under paragraphs (c) and (d).
L1:(2) For any item which is not terminated for convenience, the month in which
L0:delivery is required under the contract shall continue to apply for determining those
L0:indices with respect to the quantity of the non-terminated item.
L1:(3) If this contract is terminated for default, any price revision shall be limited to
L0:the quantity of the item which has been delivered by the Contractor and accepted by the
L0:Government prior to receipt by the Contractor of the notice of termination.
L1:(h) If the Contractor's failure to make delivery of any required quantity arises out of
L0:causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the Contractor, within
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:the meaning of the clause of this contract entitled “Default,” the quantity not delivered
L0:shall be delivered as promptly as possible after the cessation of the cause of the failure,
L0:and the delivery schedule set forth in this contract shall be amended accordingly.
L0:NOTES:
L0:1 Offeror insert the unit price and unit measure of the standard steel mill item to be
L0:used in the manufacture of the contract item.
L0:2 Offeror identify the standard steel mill item to be used in the manufacture of the
L0:contract item.
L0:3 Offeror insert best estimate of the number of days required for processing the

L0:4 Offeror identify the shop and plant in which the standard steel mill item identified

L0:5 Offeror insert the same percentage figures for the corresponding blanks in

title: 252.216-7003 Economic Price Adjustment—Wage Rates or Material Prices
content:
L0:252.216-7003 Economic Price Adjustment—Wage Rates or Material Prices
L0:Controlled by a Foreign Government.
L0:As prescribed in 216.203-470(c)(1), use the following clause:
L0:ECONOMIC PRICE ADJUSTMENT—WAGE RATES OR MATERIAL PRICES
L0:CONTROLLED BY A FOREIGN GOVERNMENT (MAR 2012)
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(a) As represented by the Contractor in its offer, the prices set forth in this
L0:contract—
L1:(1) Are based on the wage rate(s) or material price(s) established and controlled
L0:by the government of the country specified by the Contractor in its offer; and
L1:(2) Do not include contingency allowances to pay for possible increases in wage
L0:rates or material prices.
L1:(b) If wage rates or material prices are revised by the government named in
L0:paragraph (a) of this clause, the Contracting Officer shall make an equitable
L0:adjustment in the contract price and shall modify the contract to the extent that the
L0:Contractor’s actual costs of performing this contract are increased or decreased, as a
L0:direct result of the revision, subject to the following:
L1:(1) For increases in established wage rates or material prices, the increase in
L0:contract unit price(s) shall be effective on the same date that the government named in
L0:paragraph (a) of this clause increased the applicable wage rate(s) or material price(s),
L0:but only if the Contracting Officer receives the Contractor’s written request for contract
L0:adjustment within 10 days of the change. If the Contractor’s request is received later,
L0:the effective date shall be the date that the Contracting Officer received the
L0:Contractor’s request.
L1:(2) For decreases in established wage rates or material prices, the decrease in
L0:contract unit price(s) shall be effective on the same date that the government named in
L0:paragraph (a) of this clause decreased the applicable wage rate(s) or material price(s).
L0:The decrease in contract unit price(s) shall apply to all items delivered on and after the
L1:(c) No modification changing the contract unit price(s) shall be executed until the
L0:Contracting Officer has verified the applicable change in the rates or prices set by the
L0:government named in paragraph (a) of this clause. The Contractor shall make available
L0:its books and records that support a requested change in contract price.
L1:(d) Failure to agree to any adjustment shall be a dispute under the Disputes clause
L0:of this contract.
L0:(End of clause)
citation: R-DFARS 252.216-7003 — Economic Price Adjustment—Wage Rates or Material Prices

title: 252.216-7010 Postaward Debriefings for Task Orders and Delivery Orders
content:
L0:252.216-7010 Postaward Debriefings for Task Orders and Delivery Orders.
L0:As prescribed at 216.505-70, use the following clause:
L0:POSTAWARD DEBRIEFINGS FOR TASK ORDERS AND DELIVERY ORDERS
L0:(OCT 2025)
L1:(a) Postaward debriefing.
L1:(1) Upon timely request, the Government will provide a written or oral
L0:postaward debriefing for task orders or delivery orders valued at $15 million or more to
L0:the Contractor, regardless of whether the Contractor’s offer for the task order or
L0:delivery order was successful or unsuccessful, while protecting the confidential and
L0:proprietary information of other contractors. The request is considered timely if
L0:received within 3 days of notification of task order or delivery order award.
L1:(2) If a required postaward debriefing is provided—
L1:(i) The debriefed Contractor may submit additional written questions
L0:related to the required and provided debriefing within 2 business days after the date of
L0:the debriefing;
L1:(ii) The agency will respond in writing to timely submitted additional
L0:questions within 5 business days after receipt; and
L1:(iii) The postaward debriefing will not be considered to be concluded until
L0:the later of—
L0:writing; or
L1:(A) The date that the postaward debriefing is delivered, orally or in
L0:received, the date the agency delivers its written response.
L1:(B) If additional written questions related to the debriefing are timely
L1:(b) Task order or delivery order performance. The Government may suspend
L0:performance of or terminate the awarded task order or delivery order upon notice from
L0:the Government Accountability Office of a protest filed within the time periods listed in
L0:paragraphs (b)(1) through (3) of this clause, whichever is later:
L1:(1) Within 10 days after the date a task order or delivery order is issued, where
L0:the value exceeds $25 million (10 U.S.C. 3406(e)).
L1:(2) Within 5 days after a debriefing date offered to the protestor under a timely
L0:debriefing request in accordance with Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) 15.506
L0:unless an earlier debriefing date is negotiated as a result.
L1:(3) Within 5 days after a postaward debriefing under FAR 15.506 is concluded in
L0:accordance with Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement 215.506-70(b).
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216

L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:PGI 216—TYPES OF CONTRACTS
L0:PGI 216.1—SELECTING CONTRACT TYPES
L0:PGI 216.102 Negotiating contract type.
L0:Follow the procedures in the Director, Defense Procurement and Acquisition Policy
L0:memorandum dated April 1, 2016, entitled “Guidance on Using Incentive and Other Contract
L0:Types,” when selecting and negotiating the most appropriate contract type for a given
L0:procurement.
L0:PGI 216.102-70 Research and development.
L1:(1) General. There are several categories of research and development (R&D)
L0:contracts: research, exploratory development, advanced development, engineering
L0:development, and operational systems development (see DFARS 235.001 for the definition
L0:of research and development). Each category has a primary technical or functional
L0:objective. Different parts of a project may fit several categories. The contract type must fit
L0:the work required, not just the classification of the overall program.
L1:(2) Research and exploratory development.
L1:(i) Price is not necessarily the primary factor in determining the contract type.
L1:(ii) The nature of the work to be performed will usually result in a cost-plus award
L0:fee, cost-plus fixed fee term, cost-no-fee, or cost-sharing contract.
L1:(iii) If the Government and the contractor can identify and agree upon the level of
L0:contractor effort required, the contracting officer may select a firm fixed-price level-of-effort
L0:contract, except see DFARS 235.170.
L1:(iv) If the Government and the contractor agree that an incentive arrangement is
L0:desirable and capable of being evaluated after completion of the work, the contracting officer
L0:may use an incentive type contract.
L1:(3) Advanced development.
L1:(i) The nature of the work to be performed often results in a cost-plus fixed fee
L0:completion type contract.
L1:(ii) Contracting officers may select incentive contracts if—
L1:(A) Realistic and measurable targets are identified; and
L1:(B) Achievement of those targets is predictable with a reasonable degree of
L0:accuracy.
L1:(iii) Contracting officers should not use contracts with only cost incentives where—
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(A) There will be a large number of major technical changes; or
L1:(B) Actions beyond the control of the contractor may influence the contractor's
L0:achievement of cost targets.
L1:(4) Engineering development and operational systems development.
L1:(i) When selecting contract types, also consider—
L1:(A) The degree to which the project is clearly defined, which in turn affects the
L0:contractor's ability to provide accurate cost estimates;
L1:(B) The need for effort that will overlap that of earlier stages;
L1:(C) The need for firm technical direction by the Government; and
L1:(D) The degree of configuration control the Government will exercise.
L1:(ii) For development efforts, particularly for major defense systems, the preferred
L0:contract type is cost reimbursement.
L1:(iii) Contracting officers should use fixed-price type contracts when risk has been
L0:reduced to the extent that realistic pricing can occur; e.g., when a program has reached the
L0:final stages of development and technical risks are minimal, except see DFARS 235.170.
L0:PGI 216.2—FIXED-PRICE CONTRACTS
L0:PGI 216.203 Fixed-price contracts with economic price adjustment.
L0:PGI 216.203-4 Contract clauses.
L0:Contracting officers should use caution when incorporating Economic Price Adjustment
L1:(EPA) provisions in contracts. EPA provisions can result in significant and unanticipated
L0:price increases which can have major adverse impacts to a program. EPA provisions
L0:should be used only when general economic factors make the estimating of future costs too
L0:unpredictable within a fixed-price contract. The primary factors that should be considered
L0:before using an EPA provision include volatility of labor and/or material costs and contract
L0:length. In cases where cost volatility and/or contract length warrant using an EPA provision,
L0:the provision must be carefully crafted to ensure an equitable adjustment to the contract.
L0:Accordingly, contracting officers should always request assistance from their local pricing
L0:office, the Defense Contract Management Agency, or the Defense Contract Audit Agency
L0:when contemplating the use of an EPA provision.
L0:For adjustments based on cost indexes of labor or material, use the following guidelines:
L1:(1) Do not make the clause unnecessarily complex.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(2) Normally, the clause should not provide either a ceiling or a floor for adjustment
L0:unless adjustment is based on indices below the six-digit level of the Bureau of Labor
L0:Statistics (BLS)—
L1:(i) Producer Price Index;
L1:(ii) Employment Cost Index for wages and salaries, benefits, and compensation
L0:costs for aerospace industries (but see paragraphs (3) and (6) of this subsection); or
L1:(iii) North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Code.
L1:(3) DoD contracting officers may no longer use the BLS employment cost index for total
L0:compensation, aircraft manufacturing (NAICS Code 336411, formerly Standard Industrial
L0:Classification Code 3721, Aircraft) in any EPA clause in DoD contracts. This index is
L0:ineffective for use as the basis for labor cost adjustments in EPA clauses in DoD contracts.
L0:The BLS employment cost index for wages and salaries, aircraft manufacturing may still
L0:be used in EPA clauses for labor costs. If a BLS index for benefits is desired, contracting
L0:officers should use a broader based index that will smooth the effects of any large pension
L0:contributions, such as the employment cost index for benefits, total private industry. If a total
L0:compensation index is desired, contracting officers should consider the creation of a hybrid
L0:index by combining the above referenced indices at a predetermined percentage. For
L0:example, a hybrid total compensation index could consist of 68 percent employment cost
L0:index for wages and salaries, aircraft manufacturing, and 32 percent of the employment cost
L0:index for benefits, private industry.
L1:(4) Normally, the clause should cover potential economic fluctuations within the original
L0:contract period of performance using a trigger band. Unless the economic fluctuation
L0:exceeds the trigger value, no EPA clause adjustments are made.
L1:(5) The clause must accurately identify the index(es) upon which adjustments will be
L0:based.
L1:(i) It must provide for a means to adjust for appropriate economic fluctuation in the
L0:event publication of the movement of the designated index is discontinued. This might
L0:include the substitution of another index if the time remaining would justify doing so and an
L0:appropriate index is reasonably available, or some other method for repricing the remaining
L0:portion of work to be performed.
L1:(ii) Normally, there should be no need to make an adjustment if computation of the
L0:identified index is altered. However, it may be appropriate to provide for adjustment of the
L0:economic fluctuation computations in the event there is such a substantial alteration in the
L0:method of computing the index that the original intent of the parties is negated.
L1:(iii) When an index to be used is subject to revision (e.g., the BLS Producer Price
L0:Indexes), the EPA clause must specify that any economic price adjustment will be based on
L0:a revised index and must identify which revision to the index will be used.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(6) The basis of the index should not be so large and diverse that it is significantly
L0:affected by fluctuations not relevant to contract performance, but it must be broad enough to
L0:minimize the effect of any single company, including the anticipated contractor(s).
L1:(7) Construction of an index is largely dependent upon three general series published by
L0:the U.S. Department of Labor, BLS. These are the—
L1:(i) Industrial Commodities portion of the Producer Price Index;
L1:(ii) Employment Cost Index for wages and salaries, benefits, and compensation
L0:costs for aerospace industries (but see paragraphs (3) and (6) of this subsection); and
L1:(iii) NAICS Code.
L1:(8) Normally, do not use more than two indices, i.e., one for labor and one for material.
L1:(9) The clause must establish and properly identify a base period comparable to the
L0:contract periods for which adjustments are to be made as a reference point for application of
L0:an index.
L1:(10) The clause should not provide for an adjustment beyond the original contract
L0:performance period, including options. The start date for the adjustment may be the
L0:beginning of the contract or a later time, as appropriate, based on the projected rate of
L0:expenditures.
L1:(11) The expenditure profile for both labor and material should be based on a
L0:predetermined rate of expenditure (expressed as the percentage of material or labor usage
L0:as it relates to the total contract price) in lieu of actual cost incurred.
L1:(i) If the clause is to be used in a competitive acquisition, determine the labor and
L0:material allocations, with regard to both mix of labor and material and rate of expenditure by
L0:percentage, in a manner which will, as nearly as possible, approximate the average
L0:expenditure profile of all companies to be solicited so that all companies may compete on an
L0:equal basis.
L1:(ii) If the clause is to be used in a noncompetitive acquisition, the labor and material
L0:allocations may be subject to negotiation and agreement.
L1:(iii) For multiyear contracts, establish predetermined expenditure profile tables for
L0:each of the annual increments in the multiyear buy. Each of the second and subsequent
L0:year tables must be cumulative to reflect the total expenditures for all increments funded
L0:through the latest multiyear funding.
L1:(12) The clause should state the percentage of the contract price subject to price
L0:adjustment.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(i) Normally, do not apply adjustments to the profit portion of the contract.
L1:(ii) Examine the labor and material portions of the contract to exclude any areas that
L0:do not require adjustment. For example, it may be possible to exclude—
L1:(A) Subcontracting for short periods of time during the early life of the contract
L0:which could be covered by firm-fixed-priced subcontracting;
L1:(B) Certain areas of overhead, e.g., depreciation charges, prepaid insurance
L0:costs, rental costs, leases, certain taxes, and utility charges;
L1:(C) Labor costs for which a definitive union agreement exists; and
L1:(D) Those costs not likely to be affected by fluctuation in the economy.
L1:(iii) Allocate that part of the contract price subject to adjustment to specific periods of
L0:time (e.g., quarterly, semiannually, etc.) based on the most probable expenditure or
L0:commitment basis (expenditure profile).
L1:(13) The clause should provide for definite times or events that trigger price
L0:adjustments. Adjustments should be frequent enough to afford the contractor appropriate
L0:economic protection without creating a burdensome administrative effort. The adjustment
L0:period should normally range from quarterly to annually.
L1:(14) When the contract contains cost incentives, any sums paid to the contractor on
L0:account of EPA provisions must be subtracted from the total of the contractor's allowable
L0:costs for the purpose of establishing the total costs to which the cost incentive provisions
L0:apply. If the incentive arrangement is cited in percentage ranges, rather than dollar ranges,
L0:above and below target costs, structure the EPA clause to maintain the original contract
L0:incentive range in dollars.
L1:(15) The EPA clause should provide that once the labor and material allocations and the
L0:portion of the contract price subject to price adjustment have been established, they remain
L0:fixed through the life of the contract and must not be modified except in the event of
L0:significant changes in the scope of the contract. The clause should state that pricing actions
L0:pursuant to the Changes clause or other provisions of the contract will be priced as though
L0:there were no provisions for economic price adjustment. However, subsequent
L0:modifications may include a change to the delivery schedule or significantly change the
L0:amount of, or mix of, labor or material for the contract. In such cases, it may be appropriate
L0:to prospectively apply EPA coverage. This may be accomplished by—
L1:(i) Using an EPA clause that applies only to the effort covered by the modification;
L1:(ii) Revising the baseline data or period in the EPA clause for the basic contract to
L0:include the new work; or
L1:(iii) Using an entirely new EPA clause for the entire contract, including the new work.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(16) Consistent with the factors in paragraphs (1) through (15) of this subsection, it may
L0:also be appropriate to provide in the prime contract for similar EPA arrangements between
L0:the prime contractor and affected subcontractors to allocate risks properly and ensure that
L0:those subcontractors are provided similar economic protection.
L1:(17) When EPA clauses are included in contracts that do not require submission of
L0:certified cost or pricing data as provided for in FAR 15.403-2, the contracting officer must
L0:obtain adequate data to establish the baseline from which adjustments will be made. The
L0:contracting officer may require verification of the data submitted to the extent necessary to
L0:permit reliance upon the data as a reasonable baseline.
L0:PGI 216.4—INCENTIVE CONTRACTS
L0:PGI 216.401 General.
L0:PGI 216.401-1 Description.
L1:(c) Incentive contracts. See the DPCAP Price, Cost, and Finance “Pricing Topics”
L0:webpage at https://www.acq.osd.mil/asda/dpc/pcf/pricing-topics.html for links to contract
L0:incentives training, tools, and a guidebook.
L0:PGI 216.402 Award fee.
L0:PGI 216.402-2 Limitations.
L1:(c) Award-fee contracts.
L1:(i) It is DoD policy to utilize objective criteria, whenever possible, to measure
L0:contract performance. In cases where an award-fee contract must be used due to lack of
L0:objective criteria, the contracting officer must consult with the program manager and the fee
L0:determining official when developing the award-fee plan. Award-fee criteria must be linked
L0:directly to contract cost, schedule, and performance outcomes objectives.
L1:(ii) Award fees must be tied to identifiable interim outcomes, discrete events or
L0:milestones, as much as possible. Examples of such interim milestones include timely
L0:completion of preliminary design review, critical design review, and successful system
L0:demonstration. In situations where there may be no identifiable milestone for a year or
L0:more, consideration should be given to apportioning some of the award fee pool for a
L0:predetermined interim period of time based on assessing progress toward milestones. In
L0:any case, award fee provisions must clearly explain how a contractor’s performance will be
L0:evaluated.
L1:(iii) The head of the contracting activity for each defense agency must retain the
L0:D&F for (a) all acquisition category (ACAT) I or II programs, and (b) all non-ACAT I or II
L0:contracts with an estimated value of $50 million or more. The head of the contracting activity
L0:must forward the D&Fs for ACAT I programs to Defense Pricing, Contracting, and
L0:Acquisition Policy/Contract Policy directorate (DPCAP/CP) within 1 month of the end of the
L0:quarter. Copies of D&Fs on all contracts must also be included in the contract file.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:PGI 216.402-4 Cost-plus-award-fee contracts.
L1:(1) Although weighted guidelines do not apply per DFARS 216.402-4(3)(ii) when
L0:definitizing a contract action, the contracting officer must, nevertheless, separately assess
L0:and document the reduced cost risk on the contract for—
L1:(i) The period up to the date of definitization; as well as
L1:(ii) The remaining period of performance (see DFARS 217.7404-6).
L1:(2) Normally, award fee is not earned when the fee-determining official has determined
L0:that contractor performance has been submarginal or unsatisfactory.
L1:(3) The basis for all award fee determinations must be documented in the contract file.
L1:(4) The cost-plus-award-fee contract is also suitable for level of effort contracts where
L0:mission feasibility is established but measurement of achievement must be by subjective
L0:evaluation rather than objective measurement. See Table 16-1, Performance Evaluation

L0:PGI 216.403 Application of predetermined, formula-type incentives.
L0:PGI 216.403-2 Performance incentives.
L0:Contractor performance incentives should relate to specific performance areas of
L0:milestones, such as delivery or test schedules, quality controls, maintenance requirements,
L0:and reliability standards.
L0:PGI 216.404 Fixed-price incentive contracts.
L0:PGI 216.404-170 Fixed-price incentive (firm target) contracts.
L1:(1) Use of FPIF contract.
L1:(i) Not mandatory. Contracting officers must carefully consider whether to use a
L0:fixed-price incentive (firm target) (FPIF) contract, especially for acquisitions moving from
L0:development to production. DFARS does not mandate the use of FPIF for initial production
L0:and each acquisition situation must be evaluated in terms of the degree and nature of the
L0:risk presented in order to select the proper contract type.
L1:(ii) Considerations. Volume 4, chapter 1, of the Contract Pricing Reference Guide
L0:provides a detailed discussion of the considerations involved in selecting the proper contract
L0:type. For example:
L1:(A) It is not in the Government’s best interest to use FPIF when the cost risk is
L0:so great that establishing a ceiling price is unrealistic.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(B) It is also not in the Government’s best interest to use firm-fixed-price (FFP)
L0:contracts on production programs until costs have become stable. Therefore, FPIF
L0:contracts should be considered in production and sole source follow-on programs where
L0:actual costs on prior FFP contracts have varied by more than 3-4 percent from the costs
L0:considered negotiated. Contracting officers are reminded that actual costs on prior contracts
L0:for the same item or essentially the same item, regardless of contract type or data reporting
L0:requirements of the prior contract, are cost and pricing data on the pending contract, and
L0:must be obtained from the contractor on production programs when certified cost or pricing
L0:data are required.
L1:(C) For sole source major systems procurements, contracting officers should
L0:utilize FPIF contracts instead of FFP contracts unless the reasons for significant variation
L0:are well understood and actions have been taken to ensure that significant variation will not
L0:recur. In addition, when options are included as described in PGI 217.201-70, the use of
L0:FPIF contracts is both highly recommended and encouraged, because both parties will be
L0:assuming more risk in pricing multiple years of requirements.
L1:(2) Incentive arrangement. Contracting officers should consider share lines and ceiling
L0:prices for fixed-price incentive (firm target) contracts, with 120 percent ceiling and a 50/50
L0:share ratio as the point of departure for establishing the incentive arrangement. While the
L0:DFARS does not mandate the use of these share ratios or ceiling percentage, it is not
L0:unreasonable to expect that upon entering into production, risks have been mitigated to the
L0:point that the DFARS recommended point of departure for an FPIF incentive arrangement
L0:would be normal.
L1:(3) Analyzing risk.
L1:(i) Quantification of risk.
L1:(A) The first step is establishing a target cost for which the probability of an
L0:underrun and overrun are considered equal and therefore, the risks and rewards are shared
L0:equally, hence the 50/50 share is the point of departure. Equally important is determining
L0:that the contractor has a high probability of being able to accomplish the effort within a
L0:ceiling percentage of 120 percent. In accomplishing both these steps, the analysis of risk is
L0:essential.
L1:(B) Too often, risk is evaluated only in general terms without attempting to
L0:quantify the risk posed by the various elements of cost. Also, a contracting officer may
L0:incorrectly fall back on the share ratios and ceiling percentages negotiated on prior contracts
L0:or other programs, without examining the specific risks.
L1:(C) Whether being used to select the proper contract type or establishing share
L0:lines and ceiling price on an FPIF contract, the analysis of risk as it pertains to the prime
L0:contractor is key. From a contractor’s perspective, all risks, including technical and schedule
L0:risk, have financial ramifications. Technical and schedule risks, if realized, generally
L0:translate into increased effort, which means increased cost. Therefore, all risk can be
L0:translated into cost risk and quantified. Risk always has two components that must be
L0:considered in the quantification: the magnitude of the impact and the probability that it will
L0:occur.
L1:(D) When cost risk is quantified, it is much easier to establish a reasonable
L0:ceiling percentage. The ceiling percentage is applicable to the target cost on the prime
L0:contract. It is important to understand the degree of risk that various cost elements pose in
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:relation to that target cost. A discussion of the major cost elements and the risk implications
L0:follows in paragraphs (3)(ii) through (iv) of this section.
L1:(ii) Subcontracts and material cost and risk.
L1:(A) In many prime contractors’ contracts, a substantial amount of risk is borne
L0:by subcontractors, not the prime contractor, via negotiated firm-fixed-price (FFP)
L0:subcontracts. In the case of FFP subcontracts, the subcontractor is obligated to deliver at
L0:the negotiated price. The risk to the prime contractor is the supplier’s failure to perform or
L0:perform on time. Generally, that risk is considered to be low by both the prime and the
L0:subcontractor as evidenced by the FFP contract type. In addition, the prime contractor will
L0:normally have priced effort for material management or subcontract administration to ensure
L0:timely performance on the part of the suppliers. This effort may be bid directly or indirectly
L0:(e.g., as part of an overhead expense) depending on the contractor’s accounting practices.
L1:(B) The impact of negotiated FFP subcontracts on the prime contractor’s risk
L0:can be significant. A prime contract with a 120 percent ceiling price provides overrun
L0:protection to the prime contractor equal to 20 percent of the target cost on the contract.
L0:However, if FFP subcontracts represent half of the total contract cost, then half of the target
L0:cost is subject to little or no cost risk on the part of the prime contractor. Therefore, the
L0:overrun protection provided by 20 percent of the target cost is really closer to 40 percent
L0:protection of the prime’s cost that is truly at risk to the prime contractor, which likely is
L0:significantly overstated. Thus, a ceiling price less than 120 percent in this risk situation
L0:would be more appropriate.
L1:(C) For subcontracts that have not yet been negotiated between the prime and
L0:subcontractor at the time of negotiation of the prime contract, the degree of risk is essentially
L0:limited to the difference between the price proposed by the subcontractor and the
L0:subcontract value included in the prime contractor’s proposal.
L1:(D) For subcontracts that are not FFP, the risk to the prime is based on the risk
L0:represented by the subcontractors’ contractual relationship with the prime. If the
L0:subcontract is FPIF and has a 50/50 share ratio and 120 percent ceiling, the prime’s risk is
L0:50 percent of each dollar of overrun up to the ceiling amount. An analysis of the
L0:subcontractor’s risk would be necessary to determine the probability of reaching the ceiling
L0:price.
L1:(iii) Direct labor cost and risk.
L1:(A) The risk in direct labor is in the hours needed to perform the effort and the
L0:risk in the labor rates paid to employees. There is generally little risk in the direct labor rates.
L0:However, there are various levels of risk in the direct labor hours needed by the prime
L0:contractor to accomplish the contract requirements. This risk can be driven by a number of
L0:factors including technical complexity, schedule constraints, or availability of personnel,
L0:parts, or tooling. Risks vary by task and the key is to identify the major tasks and assess the
L0:“what if” impact at the total contract cost level.
L1:(B) Schedule is often correctly cited as a risk factor, but it is important to
L0:understand and quantify the probability and impact of a potential schedule slip. Generally,
L0:any schedule slip can only affect the prime contractor’s in-house cost. Therefore, any
L0:schedule impact should be assessed on the impact it would have on the prime contractor’s
L0:performance of its tasks.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L1:(C) However, it is wrong to assume the worst-case scenario that a schedule
L0:delay results in an extension of the entire prime contractor workforce for the period of the
L0:delay. A responsible contractor will take steps to minimize both the delay and the impact of
L0:that delay. For instance, a production schedule assumes an optimal sequencing of tasks
L0:which presumes the timely arrival and availability of parts from suppliers or other in-house
L0:sources. A delay in receiving parts as planned could require a resequencing of tasks and
L0:could adversely affect the efficiency of performing a number of tasks, but it will not cause the
L0:entire workforce to be idle during the delay.
L1:(iv) Indirect (e.g., overhead) cost and risk. Overhead and other indirect costs (e.g.,
L0:general and administrative expense) can represent a significant portion of the prime
L0:contractor’s in-house cost. Indirect expense (hereafter referred to as overhead) poses
L0:potential cost growth risk or the opportunity for cost reduction from the following two
L0:perspectives:
L1:(A) Actual overhead rate. (1) First, the actual overhead rate could be different
L0:than that proposed. Proposed overhead rates, even those covered by a forward pricing rate
L0:agreement, are based on forecasts of overhead expenses and the bases to which they are
L0:applied. The final overhead rate that is actually applied (charged) to a contract will be based
L0:on the actual overhead expenses and the actual base, each of which could be considerably
L0:different than estimated. The net effect could be a higher or lower overhead rate than
L0:estimated.
L1:(2) In general, the risk in an overhead rate tends to be driven more by
L0:fluctuations in the base than in the expenses. This is because overhead expenses are
L0:made up of expenses that consist of “fixed” (e.g., depreciation) and variable (e.g., fringe
L0:benefits) in nature. When the actual base turns out to be lower than the estimated base, the
L0:fixed costs are spread over a smaller base resulting in a higher overhead rate. In general, if
L0:the actual base is greater than estimated, a lower overhead rate will result.
L1:(3) In assessing this risk, the contracting officer should consider the
L0:contractor’s ability to predict overhead rates based on comparing proposed versus actual
L0:rates for prior years. In making this comparison, it is important to do so in a manner
L0:consistent with the proposal being reviewed. For instance, if the majority of overhead costs
L0:on the proposal being reviewed occur two years in the future, the comparison should look at
L0:the contractor’s accuracy in predicting overhead rates two years in advance. For example,
L0:in looking at the 2009 actual overhead rate, what did the contractor propose for 2009 in its
L0:2007 forward pricing rate proposal?
L1:(B) Actual base cost. If the actual base cost on the contract (e.g., direct labor
L0:dollars) is different than that proposed, the contract will be charged overhead costs
L0:according to the actual base costs on that contract. If the contractor overruns direct labor,
L0:even if the actual labor overhead rate was the same as proposed, that rate would be applied
L0:to a higher base resulting in increased overhead dollars on that contract. The opposite
L0:would be true if the contractor underruns direct labor on the contract. Since this aspect of
L0:risk is tied to the base cost on the contract, the risk is the same as it is for those base costs
L0:(e.g., direct labor, material).
L0:PGI 216.404-2 Fixed-price incentive (successive targets) contracts.
L0:The formula specified in FAR 16.404-2(a)(3) does not apply for the life of the contract. It is
L0:used to fix the firm target profit for the contract. To provide an incentive consistent with the
L0:circumstances, the formula should reflect the relative risk involved in establishing an
L0:incentive arrangement where cost and pricing information were not sufficient to permit the
L0:negotiation of firm targets at the outset.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 16
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 216
L0:PGI 216.405 Cost-plus-incentive-fee contracts.
L0:Give appropriate weight to basic acquisition objectives in negotiating the range of fee and
L0:the fee adjustment formula. For example—
L1:(1) In an initial product development contract, it may be appropriate to provide for
L0:relatively small adjustments in fee tied to the cost incentive feature, but provide for significant
L0:adjustments if the contractor meets or surpasses performance targets; and
L1:(2) In subsequent development and test contracts, it may be appropriate to negotiate an
L0:incentive formula tied primarily to the contractor's success in controlling costs.

title: 217.102 Definitions
content:
L0:217.102 Definitions.
L0:As used in this subpart—
L0:“Advance procurement” means an exception to the full funding policy that allows
L0:acquisition of long lead time items (advance long lead acquisition) or economic order
L0:quantities (EOQ) of items (advance EOQ acquisition) in a fiscal year in advance of that
L0:in which the related end item is to be acquired. Advance procurements may include
L0:materials, parts, components, and effort that must be funded in advance to maintain a
L0:planned production schedule.
L0:“Congressional defense committees,” means—
L1:(1) The Committee on Armed Services of the Senate;
L1:(2) The Committee on Appropriations of the Senate;
L1:(3) The Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations of the
L0:Senate;
L1:(4) The Committee on Armed Services of the House of Representatives;
L1:(5) The Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives; and
L1:(6) The Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations of the House
L0:of Representatives.
L0:“Military installation” means a base, camp, post, station, yard, center, or other activity
L0:under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of a military department or, in the case of an
L0:activity in a foreign country, under the operational control of the Secretary of a military
L0:department or the Secretary of Defense (10 U.S.C. 2801(c)(4)).

title: 217.103-170 Multiyear contract cost analysis
content:
L0:217.103-170 Multiyear contract cost analysis.
L0:Before awarding a multiyear contract, the head of the agency must compare the cost of
L0:that contract to the cost of an annual procurement approach, using a present value
L0:analysis. Only award the multiyear contract if the analysis shows that it will result in a
L0:lower cost (10 U.S.C. 3501(l)(7); section 8008(a) of Pub. L. 105-56, and similar sections
L0:in subsequent DoD appropriations acts).

title: 217.103-171 Multiyear contracts for services
content:
L0:217.103-171 Multiyear contracts for services.
L1:(a) The head of the agency has the authority to enter into multiyear contracts for a
L0:period of not more than 5 years for covered services and items of supply relating to such
L0:services, even though funds are limited by statute to obligation only during the fiscal
L0:year for which they were appropriated (10 U.S.C. 3531(a). Covered services are—
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(1) Operation, maintenance, and support of facilities and installations;
L1:(2) Maintenance or modification of aircraft, ships, vehicles, and other highly
L0:complex military equipment;
L1:(3) Specialized training requiring high quality instructor skills (e.g., training for
L0:pilots and aircrew members or foreign language training);
L1:(4) Base services (e.g., ground maintenance, in-plane refueling, bus
L0:transportation, and refuse collection and disposal); and
L1:(5) Environmental remediation services for—
L1:(i) An active military installation;
L1:(ii) A military installation being closed or realigned under a base closure
L0:law as defined in 10 U.S.C. 2667(h)(2); or
L1:(iii) A site formerly used by DoD (10 U.S.C. 3531(b)).
L1:(b) See PGI 217.103-171(b) for considerations for using multiyear contracts for
L0:services.
L1:(c) Before entering into a multiyear contract for services, the head of the agency
L0:must make a written determination that
L1:(1) There will be a continuing requirement for the services that is consistent
L0:with current plans for the proposed contract period;
L1:(2) Furnishing the services will require
L1:(i) A substantial initial investment in plant or equipment; or
L1:(ii) The incurrence of substantial contingent liabilities for the assembly,
L0:training, or transportation of a specialized work force; and
L1:(3) Using a multiyear contract will promote the best interests of the United
L0:States by encouraging effective competition and promoting economies in operations (10
L0:U.S.C. 3531(a)).
L1:(d) The head of an agency may not initiate a multiyear contract for services if the
L0:value of the multiyear contract exceeds $900 million unless specifically authorized by
L0:law (10 U.S.C. 3531(d)(2)).

title: 217.103-172 Multiyear contracts for supplies
content:
L0:217.103-172 Multiyear contracts for supplies.
L1:(a) This section applies to all multiyear contracts for supplies, including weapon
L0:systems and other multiyear acquisitions specifically authorized by law (10 U.S.C.
L0:3501).
L1:(b) Multiyear contracts in amounts exceeding $900 million must be specifically
L0:authorized by law in an act other than an appropriations act (10 U.S.C. 3501(i)(1)).
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(c) The head of the agency may not initiate a multiyear procurement contract for
L0:any system (or component thereof) if the value of the multiyear contract exceeds $900
L0:million unless authority for the contract is specifically provided in an appropriations act
L0:(10 U.S.C. 3501(l)(3)).
L1:(d) The head of the agency must not enter into a multiyear contract unless—
L1:(1) The Secretary of Defense has submitted to Congress a budget request for
L0:full funding of units to be procured through the contract;
L1:(2) In the case of a contract for procurement of aircraft, the budget request
L0:includes full funding of procurement funds for production beyond advance procurement
L0:activities of aircraft units to be produced in the fiscal year covered by the budget;
L1:(3) Cancellation provisions in the contract do not include consideration of the
L0:contractor’s recurring manufacturing costs associated with the production of unfunded
L0:units to be delivered under the contract;
L1:(4) The contract provides that payments to the contractor under the contract
L0:must not be made in advance of incurred costs on funded units; and
L1:(5) The contract does not provide for a price adjustment based on a failure to
L0:award a follow-on contract (section 8010 of Division C, Title VIII, of the Consolidated
L0:and Further Continuing Appropriations Act, 2015 (Pub. L. 113-235) and similar
L0:sections in subsequent DoD appropriations acts).
L2:(e)(1) The head of the agency must not enter into or extend a multiyear contract
L0:that exceeds $900 million (when entered into or extended) until the Secretary of
L0:Defense identifies the contract and any extension in a report submitted to the
L0:congressional defense committees (10 U.S.C. 3501(l)(5)).
L1:(2) In addition, for contracts equal to or greater than $900 million, the head of
L0:the contracting activity must determine that the conditions required by paragraphs
L3:(g)(2)(i) through (vii) of this section will be met by such contract, in accordance with the
L0:Secretary’s certification and determination required by paragraph (g)(2) of this section.
L1:(f) The head of the agency may enter into a multiyear contract for—

L0:weapon system (10 U.S.C. 3501(h)(1)); and
L1:(2) Advance procurement of components, parts, and materials necessary to
L0:manufacture a weapon system, including advance procurement to achieve economic lot
L0:purchases or more efficient production rates (see paragraphs (g)(3) and (4) of this

L0:initiating an advance procurement, the contracting officer must verify that it is
L0:consistent with DoD policy (e.g., the full funding policy in Volume 2A, chapter 1, of DoD
L0:7000.14-R, Financial Management Regulation).
L1:(g) The head of the agency must ensure that the following conditions are satisfied
L0:before awarding a multiyear contract for a defense acquisition program that has been
L0:specifically authorized by law to be carried out using multiyear contract authority:
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(1) The multiyear exhibits required by DoD 7000.14-R, Financial Management
L0:Regulation, are included in the agency’s budget estimate submission and the
L0:President’s budget request.
L1:(2) The Secretary of Defense certifies to Congress in writing, by no later than 30
L0:days before entry into such contracts, that each of the conditions in paragraphs (g)(2)(i)
L0:through (vii) of this section is satisfied (10 U.S.C. 3501(i)(3)).
L1:(i) The Secretary has determined that each of the requirements in FAR
L0:17.103-1, paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(7), will be met by such contract and has
L0:provided the basis for such determination to the congressional defense committees (10
L0:U.S.C. 3501(i)(3)(A)).

L0:was made after the completion of a cost analysis performed by the Defense Cost and
L0:Resource Center of the Department of Defense and such analysis supports the findings

L1:(iii) The system being acquired pursuant to such contract has not been

L0:consistent with the authorization for such contract) will be awarded (10 U.S.C.

L0:such contract have been delivered at or within the most current estimates of the
L0:program acquisition unit cost or procurement unit cost for such system to determine
L0:that current estimates of such unit costs are realistic (10 U.S.C. 3501(i)(3)(D)).
L1:(v) Sufficient funds will be available in the fiscal year in which the contract
L0:will be awarded to perform the contract, and the future-years defense program for such
L0:fiscal year will include the funding required to execute the program without
L0:cancellation (10 U.S.C. 3501(i)(3)(E)).
L1:(vi) The contract is a fixed price type contract (10 U.S.C. 3501(i)(3)(F)).
L1:(vii) The proposed multiyear contract provides for production at not less
L0:than minimum economic rates, given the existing tooling and facilities (10 U.S.C.
L0:3501(i)(3)(G)). The head of the agency must submit to OUSD(C)(P/B) information
L0:supporting the agency’s determination that this requirement has been met.
L1:(viii) The head of the agency must submit information supporting this
L0:certification to OUSD(C)(P/B) for transmission to Congress through the Secretary of
L0:Defense.

title: 217.103-174 Multiyear contracts for electricity from renewable energy
content:
L0:217.103-174 Multiyear contracts for electricity from renewable energy
L0:sources.
L1:(a) The head of the contracting activity may enter into a contract for a period not to
L0:exceed 10 years for the purchase of electricity from sources of renewable energy, as that
L0:term is defined in section 203(b)(2) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C.
L0:15852(b)(2)).
L1:(b) The head of the contracting activity may exercise the authority in paragraph (a)
L0:of this section to enter into a contract for a period in excess of five years only if the head
L0:of the contracting activity determines, on the basis of a business case analysis prepared
L0:by the requiring activity, that—
L1:(1) The proposed purchase of electricity under such contract is cost effective;
L0:and
L1:(2) It would not be possible to purchase electricity from the source in an
L0:economical manner without the use of a contract for a period in excess of five years.
L1:(c) Nothing in this section shall be construed to preclude the DoD from using other
L0:multiyear contracting authority of DoD to purchase renewable energy.
L1:(d) See PGI 217.103-174 for a business case analysis template and guidance.

title: 217.203-70 Solicitation provisions and contract clauses

title: 217.601 Definitions
content:
L0:217.601 Definitions.
L0:As used in this subpart—
L0:“Assisted acquisition” means the type of interagency contracting through which
L0:acquisition officials of a non-DoD agency award a contract or a task or delivery order for
L0:the acquisition of supplies or services on behalf of DoD.
L0:“Direct acquisition” means the type of interagency contracting through which DoD
L0:orders a supply or service from a Governmentwide acquisition contract maintained by a
L0:non-DoD agency.
L0:“Governmentwide acquisition contract” means a task or delivery order contract that-
L1:(i) Is entered into by a non-defense agency; and
L1:(ii) May be used as the contract under which property or services are procured for
L0:one or more other departments or agencies of the Federal Government.

title: 217.670 Procedures
content:
L0:217.670 Procedures.
L0:Departments and agencies must establish and maintain procedures for reviewing and
L0:approving orders placed for supplies and services under non-DoD contracts, whether
L0:through direct acquisition or assisted acquisition, when the amount of the order exceeds
L0:the simplified acquisition threshold. These procedures must include—
L1:(a) Evaluating whether using a non-DoD contract for the acquisition is in the best
L0:interest of DoD. Factors to be considered include—
L1:(1) Satisfying customer requirements;
L1:(2) Schedule;
L1:(3) Cost effectiveness (taking into account discounts and fees). In order to
L0:ensure awareness of the total cost of fees associated with use of a non-DoD contract,
L0:follow the procedures at PGI 217.670(a)(3); and
L1:(4) Contract administration (including oversight);
L1:(b) Determining that the tasks to be accomplished or supplies to be provided are
L0:within the scope of the contract to be used;
L1:(c) Reviewing funding to ensure that it is used in accordance with appropriation
L0:limitations; and
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(d) Collecting and reporting data on the use of assisted acquisition for analysis.
L0:Follow the reporting requirements in 204.301.

title: 217.7000 Scope of subpart
content:
L0:217.7000 Scope of subpart.
L0:This subpart prescribes policy and procedures for exchange of non-excess personal
L0:property concurrent with an acquisition. 40 U.S.C. 503 permits exchange of personal
L0:property and application of the exchange allowance to the acquisition of similar
L0:property. This subpart does not authorize the sale of non-excess personal property.

title: 217.7001 Definitions
content:
L0:217.7001 Definitions.
L0:As used in this subpart—
L1:(a) “Exchange (trade-in) property” means property which—
L1:(1) Is not excess but is eligible for replacement (because of obsolescence,
L0:unserviceability, or other reason); and
L1:(2) Is applied as whole or partial payment toward the acquisition of similar
L0:items (i.e., items designed and constructed for the same purpose).
L1:(b) “Property” means items that fall within one of the generic categories listed in
L0:DoD Manual 4140.01, Volume 9, DoD Supply Chain Materiel Management Procedures:
L0:Materiel Programs.

title: 217.7002 Policy
content:
L0:217.7002 Policy.
L0:DoD policy is to exchange, rather than replace, eligible non-excess property whenever
L0:exchange promotes economical and efficient program accomplishment. Exchange
L0:policy, authority, and applicability are governed by—
L1:(a) The Federal Property Management Regulations issued by the Administrator of
L0:the General Services Administration; and
L1:(b) DoD Manual 4140.01, Volume 9, DoD Supply Chain Materiel Management
L0:Procedures: Materiel Programs.

title: 217.7101 Definitions
content:
L0:217.7101 Definitions.
L1:(a) “Master agreement for repair and alteration of vessels”—

L0:activity and a contractor that—

L0:contracts for repairs, alterations, and/or additions to vessels; and
L1:(B) Contemplates separate future contracts that will incorporate by

L0:agreement.
L1:(2) Is not a contract.

L1:(1) Is a fixed price contract incorporating, by reference or attachment, a master
L0:agreement for repair and alteration of vessels;
L1:(2) May include clauses pertaining to subjects not covered by the master
L0:agreement; but applicable to the job order being awarded; and

title: 217.7102 General
content:
L0:217.7102 General.
L1:(a) Activities will enter into master agreements for repair and alteration of vessels
L0:with all prospective contractors located within the United States or its outlying areas,
L0:which—
L1:(1) Request ship repair work; and
L1:(2) Possess the organization and facilities to perform the work satisfactorily.
L0:(Issuance of a master agreement does not indicate approval of the contractor's facility
L0:for any particular acquisition and is not an affirmative determination of responsibility
L0:under FAR subpart 9.1 for any particular acquisition.)
L1:(b) Activities may use master agreements in work with prospective contractors
L0:located outside the United States and its outlying areas.
L1:(c) Activities may issue job orders under master agreements to effect repairs,
L0:alterations, and/or additions to vessels belonging to foreign governments.
L1:(1) Contractors shall treat vessels of a foreign government as if they were
L0:vessels of the U.S. Government when requested by the contracting officer.
L1:(2) Identify the vessel and the foreign government in the solicitation and job
L0:order.

title: 217.7300 Scope
content:
L0:217.7300 Scope.
L0:This subpart implements 10 U.S.C. 4753. It contains policy and procedures for
L0:requiring contractors to identify the actual manufacturer of supplies furnished to DoD.
subpart: SUBPART 217.73 — IDENTIFICATION OF SOURCES OF SUPPLY

title: 217.7301 Policy
content:
L0:217.7301 Policy.
L0:Contractors are required to identify their sources of supply in contracts for supplies.
L0:Contractor identification of sources of supply enables solicitation, in subsequent
L0:acquisitions, of actual manufacturers or other suppliers of items. This enhances
L0:competition and potentially avoids payment of additional costs for no significant added
L0:value.
subpart: SUBPART 217.73 — IDENTIFICATION OF SOURCES OF SUPPLY

title: 217.7302 Procedures
content:
L0:217.7302 Procedures.
L1:(a) Whenever practicable, include a requirement for contractor identification of
L0:sources of supply in contracts for the delivery of supplies. Contractors are required to
L0:identify—
L1:(1) The item's actual manufacturer or producer, or all the contractor's sources
L0:for the item;
L1:(2) The item's national stock number, if applicable;
L1:(3) The item identification number used by—
L1:(i) The actual manufacturer or producer of the item; or
L1:(ii) Each of the contractor's sources for the item; and
L1:(4) The source of any technical data delivered under the contract.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(b) The requirement in paragraph (a) of this section does not apply to contracts that
L0:are—
L1:(1) For commercial products; or
L1:(2) Valued at or below the simplified acquisition threshold.

title: 217.7400 Scope
content:
L0:217.7400 Scope.
L0:This subpart prescribes policies and procedures implementing 10 U.S.C. 3371, et seq.

title: 217.7401 Definitions
content:
L0:217.7401 Definitions.
L0:As used in this subpart—
L0:“Contract action” means an action which results in a contract.
L1:(1) It includes contract modifications for additional supplies or services.
L1:(2) It includes task orders and delivery orders.
L1:(3) It does not include change orders, administrative changes, funding
L0:modifications, or any other contract modifications that are within the scope and under
L0:the terms of the contract, e.g., engineering change proposals, value engineering change
L0:proposals, and over and above work requests as described in subpart 217.77.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L0:“Definitization” means the agreement on, or determination of, contract terms,
L0:specifications, and price, which converts the undefinitized contract action to a definitive
L0:contract.
L0:“Qualifying proposal” means a proposal that contains sufficient information to
L0:enable DoD to conduct meaningful analyses and audits of the information contained in
L0:the proposal.
L0:“Undefinitized contract action” means any contract action for which the contract
L0:terms, specifications, or price are not agreed upon before performance is begun under
L0:the action. Examples are letter contracts, orders under basic ordering agreements, and
L0:provisioned item orders, for which the price has not been agreed upon before
L0:performance has begun.

title: 217.7402 Exceptions
content:
L0:217.7402 Exceptions.
L1:(a) The following undefinitized contract actions (UCAs) are not subject to this
L0:subpart. However, the contracting officer will apply the policy and procedures to them
L0:to the maximum extent practicable (also see paragraph (b) of this section):
L1:(1) Purchases at or below the simplified acquisition threshold.
L1:(2) Special access programs.
L1:(3) Congressionally mandated long-lead procurement contracts.
L1:(b) If the contracting officer determines that it is impracticable to adhere to the
L0:procedures of this subpart for a particular contract action that falls within one of the
L0:categories in paragraph (a) of this section, the contracting officer will provide prior
L0:notice, through agency channels, electronically via email to the Principal Director,
L0:Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy (Contract Policy), at

title: 217.7403 Policy
content:
L0:217.7403 Policy.
L0:DoD policy is that undefinitized contract actions will—
L1:(a) Be used only when—
L1:(1) The negotiation of a definitive contract action is not possible in sufficient
L0:time to meet the Government's requirements; and
L1:(2) The Government's interest demands that the contractor be given a binding
L0:commitment so that contract performance can begin immediately.
L1:(b) Be as complete and definite as practicable under the particular circumstances.

title: 217.7404 Limitations
content:
L0:217.7404 Limitations.
L0:See PGI 217.7404 for additional guidance on obtaining approval to authorize use of an
L0:undefinitized contact action, documentation requirements, and other limitations on
L0:their use.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(a) Foreign military sales contracts.
L1:(1) A contracting officer may not enter into a UCA for a foreign military sale
L0:unless—
L1:(i) The UCA provides for agreement upon contractual terms, specifications,
L0:and price by the end of the 180-day period beginning on the date on which the
L0:contractor submits a qualifying proposal; and
L1:(ii) The contracting officer obtains approval from the head of the contracting
L0:activity to enter into a UCA in accordance with 217.7404-1.
L1:(2) The head of the contracting activity may waive the requirements of
L0:paragraph (a)(1) of this section, if a waiver is necessary in order to support any of the
L0:following operations:
L1:(i) A contingency operation.
L1:(ii) A humanitarian or peacekeeping operation.
L1:(b) Unilateral definitization by a contracting officer. Any UCA with a value greater
L0:than $50 million may not be unilaterally definitized until—
L1:(1) The earlier of—
L1:(i) The end of the 180-day period, beginning on the date on which the
L0:contractor submits a qualifying proposal to definitize the contractual terms,
L0:specifications, and price; or
L1:(ii) The date on which the amount of funds expended under the contractual
L0:action is equal to more than 50 percent of the negotiated overall not-to-exceed price for
L0:the contractual action;
L1:(2) The head of the contracting activity, without power of redelegation, approves
L0:the definitization in writing;
L1:(3) The contracting officer provides a copy of the written approval to the
L0:contractor; and
L1:(4) A period of 30 calendar days has elapsed after the written approval is
L0:provided to the contractor.

title: 217.7404-1 Authorization
content:
L0:217.7404-1 Authorization.
L0:The contracting officer will obtain approval from the head of the contracting activity
L0:before—
L1:(a) Entering into a UCA. The request for approval must fully explain the need to
L0:begin performance before definitization, including the adverse impact on agency
L0:requirements resulting from delays in beginning performance.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217
L1:(b) Including requirements for non-urgent spare parts and support equipment in a
L0:UCA. The request should show that inclusion of the non-urgent items is consistent
L0:with good business practices and in the best interest of the United States.
L1:(c) Modifying the scope of a UCA when performance has already begun. The
L0:request should show that the modification is consistent with good business practices
L0:and in the best interests of the United States.

title: 217.7404-2 Price ceiling
content:
L0:217.7404-2 Price ceiling.
L0:UCAs must include a not-to-exceed price. See PGI 217.7404-2 for additional guidance
L0:on establishing the not-to-exceed price.

title: 217.7404-3 Definitization schedule
content:
L0:217.7404-3 Definitization schedule.
L1:(a) UCAs must contain definitization schedules that provide for definitization by the
L0:earlier of—
L1:(1) The date that is 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal.
L0:This date may not be extended beyond an additional 90 days without a written
L0:determination by the head of the contracting activity without power of redelegation, the
L0:commander of the combatant command concerned, or the Under Secretary of Defense
L0:for Acquisition and Sustainment that it is in the best interests of the military
L0:department or the defense agency, the combatant command, or the Department of
L0:Defense, respectively, to continue the actions; or
L1:(2) The date on which the amount of funds obligated under the contract action
L0:is equal to more than 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price.
L2:(b)(1) Submission of a qualifying proposal in accordance with the definitization
L0:schedule is a material element of the contract. If the contractor does not submit a
L0:qualifying proposal in accordance with the contract definitization schedule,
L0:notwithstanding FAR 52.216-26, Payments of Allowable Costs Before Definitization, the
L0:contracting officer may withhold an amount necessary to protect the interests of the
L0:Government, not to exceed 5 percent of all subsequent financing requests, or take other
L0:appropriate actions (e.g., documenting the noncompliance in the contractor’s past
L0:performance evaluation or terminating the contract for default).
L1:(2) Contracting officers must document in the contract file the justification for
L0:withholding or not withholding payments if the qualifying proposal was not submitted
L0:in accordance with the contract definitization schedule.

title: 217.7404-4 Limitations on obligations
content:
L0:217.7404-4 Limitations on obligations.
L1:(a) The Government must not obligate more than 50 percent of the not-to-exceed
L0:price before definitization. However, if a contractor submits a qualifying proposal
L0:before 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price has been obligated by the Government, then
L0:the limitation on obligations before definitization may be increased to no more than 75
L0:percent (see 232.102-70 for coverage on provisional delivery payments).
L1:(b) In determining the appropriate amount to obligate, the contracting officer will
L0:assess the contractor’s proposal for the undefinitized period and will obligate funds only
L0:in an amount consistent with the contractor’s requirements for the undefinitized period.
L0:Revolutionary Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Overhaul Part 17
L0:Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) Part 217

title: 217.7404-5 Exceptions
content:
L0:217.7404-5 Exceptions.
L1:(a) The limitations in 217.7404-2, 217.7404-3, and 217.7404-4 do not apply to UCAs
L0:for the purchase of initial spares.
L1:(b) The head of an agency may waive the limitations in 217.7404(a), 217.7404-2,
L0:217.7404-3, and 217.7404-4 for UCAs if the head of the agency determines that the
L0:waiver is necessary to support—
L1:(1) A contingency operation; or

title: 217.7404-6 Allowable profit
content:
L0:217.7404-6 Allowable profit.
L0:When the final price of a UCA is negotiated after a substantial portion of the required
L0:performance has been completed, the head of the contracting activity will ensure the
L0:profit allowed reflects—
L1:(a) Any reduced cost risk to the contractor for costs incurred during contract
L0:performance before negotiation of the final price. However, if a contractor submits a
L0:qualifying proposal to definitize a UCA, and the contracting officer for such action
L0:definitizes the contract after the end of the 180-day period beginning on the date on
L0:which the contractor submitted the qualifying proposal, the profit allowed on the
L0:contract must accurately reflect the cost risk of the contractor as such risk existed on
L0:the date the contractor submitted the qualifying proposal;
L1:(b) Any reduced cost risk to the contractor for costs expected to be incurred during
L0:performance of the remainder of the contract after negotiation of the final price; and
L1:(c) The requirements at 215.409 (see PGI 217.7404-6). Document the risk
L0:assessment in the price negotiation memorandum.

title: 217.7505 Limitations on price increases
content:
L0:217.7505 Limitations on price increases.
L0:This section provides implementing guidance for Section 1215 of Pub. L. 98-94 (10
L0:U.S.C. 2452 note).
L1:(a) Do not award, on a sole source basis, a contract for any centrally managed
L0:replenishment part when the price of the part has increased by 25 percent or more over
L0:the most recent 12-month period.
L1:(1) Before computing the percentage difference between the current price and
L0:the prior price, adjust for quantity, escalation, and other factors necessary to achieve
L0:comparability.
L1:(2) Departments and agencies may specify an alternate percentage or
L0:percentages for contracts at or below the simplified acquisition threshold.
L1:(b) The contracting officer may award a contract for a part, the price of which
L0:exceeds the limitation in paragraph (a) of this section, if the contracting officer certifies
L0:in writing to the head of the contracting activity before award that—
L1:(1) The contracting officer has evaluated the price of the part and concluded
L0:that the price increase is fair and reasonable; or
L1:(2) The national security interests of the United States require purchase of the
L0:part despite the price increase.
L1:(c) The fact that a particular price has not exceeded the limitation in paragraph (a)
L0:of this section does not relieve the contracting officer of the responsibility for obtaining a
L0:fair and reasonable price.
L1:(d) Contracting officers may include a provision in sole source solicitations requiring
L0:that the offeror supply with its proposal, price and quantity data on any Government
L0:orders for the replenishment part issued within the most recent 12 months.
